claim: A collection of 96 B. cinerea isolates was used for infection experiments on Arabidopsis.
source: We assessed the impact of genetic diversity in pathogen and host by utilization of a collection of 96 isolates infection on Arabidopsis wild-type and two mutants with jasmonate or salicylic acid compromised immunities.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the use of 96 isolates in the experimental design.

claim: Ten B. cinerea gene co-expression networks (GCNs) were identified that encode known or novel virulence mechanisms.
source: We identified ten B. cinereagene co-expression networks (GCNs) that encode known or novel virulence mechanisms.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the identification of ten GCNs from the analysis.

claim: A dual interaction network was constructed by combining four host- and ten pathogen-GCNs.
source: Construction of a dual interaction network by combining four host- and ten pathogen-GCNs revealed potential connections between the fungal and plant GCNs.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the construction of a dual interaction network.

claim: B. cinerea is a necrotrophic generalist pathogen that attacks a broad range of diverse plant hosts, including dicots, gymnosperms, and even bryophytes.
source: B. cinerea is a necrotrophic generalist pathogen that attacks a broad range of diverse plant hosts, including dicots, gymnosperms, and even bryophytes (Williamson et al., 2007).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Williamson et al., 2007.

claim: B. cinerea can cause severe pre- and post-harvest losses in many crops.
source: This necrotrophic pathogen is endemic throughout the world and can cause severe pre- and post-harvest losses in many crops.
evidence: The statement is based on established knowledge about B. cinerea's agricultural impact.

claim: The Arabidopsis mutant coi1-1 is compromised in jasmonate defense signaling.
source: Isolates were inoculated on Arabidopsis Col-0 wild-type (WT) in conjunction with immune-deficient hormone mutants coi1-1 (jasmonate defense signaling) and npr1-1 (salicylic acid defense signaling).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that coi1-1 is compromised in jasmonate defense signaling.

claim: The Arabidopsis mutant npr1-1 is compromised in salicylic acid defense signaling.
source: Isolates were inoculated on Arabidopsis Col-0 wild-type (WT) in conjunction with immune-deficient hormone mutants coi1-1 (jasmonate defense signaling) and npr1-1 (salicylic acid defense signaling).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that npr1-1 is compromised in salicylic acid defense signaling.

claim: Transcriptome analysis was conducted at 16 hours post-infection (HPI).
source: From individual infected leaves, both Arabidopsis and B. cinerea transcripts at 16 hr post-infection (HPI) were simultaneously measured.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the time point for transcriptome measurement.

claim: 9284 predicted B. cinerea gene models were identified with a minimum of either 30 gene counts in one isolate or 300 gene counts across 96 isolates.
source: Mapping the dual-transcriptome reads against the B. cinerea reference genome (B05.10), we identified 9284 predicted gene models with a minimum of either 30 gene counts in one isolate or 300 gene counts across 96 isolates.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of identified gene models and the thresholds used.

claim: The identified 9284 genes correspond to approximately 79% of the 11,701 predicted encoding genes in B05.10 reference genome.
source: The total of identified genes corresponds to ~ 79% of the 11,701 predicted encoding genes in B05.10 reference genome (Van Kan et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the percentage and cites the reference genome source.

claim: The fraction of total reads that map to B. cinerea is a biologically relevant indicator of pathogen virulence.
source: Given this, we hypothesized that the fraction of total reads that map to B. cinerea might be a biologically relevant indicator of pathogen virulence (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this hypothesis.

claim: B. cinerea transcript abundance at 16HPI showed a significant partial correlation with lesion development at 72HPI in WT Col-0 (R2 = 0.1101, p-value=0.0016).
source: Comparing B. cinerea transcript abundance at 16HPI to lesion development at 72HPI revealed a significant partial correlation in the WT Col-0 (R2 = 0.1101, p-value=0.0016, Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical values and references Figure 1 showing the correlation.

claim: In npr1-1 and coi1-1 mutants, early transcriptomic activities of most B. cinerea isolates were more vigorous compared to WT.
source: In contrast to WT, the early transcriptomic activities of most B. cinerea isolates were more vigorous in the two Arabidopsis mutants, resulting in a significant curvilinear relationship between total fraction of B. cinerea reads and final lesion area (p-value=3.914e-07, p-value=0.0001, respectively, Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states increased transcriptomic activity in mutants with statistical support.

claim: The total reads fraction was better correlated with final lesion area in coi1-1 (R2 = 0.2562) than either WT (R2 = 0.1101) or npr1-1 (R2 = 0.161).
source: Interestingly, the total reads fraction was better correlated with final lesion area in coi1-1 (R2 = 0.2562) than either WT (R2 = 0.1101) or npr1-1 (R2 = 0.161).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides R2 values for comparison across genotypes.

claim: 8603 B. cinerea transcripts were significantly influenced by genetic variation in the pathogen.
source: Of the 9284 detectable B. cinerea transcripts, 8603 and 5244 transcripts were significantly influenced by genetic variation in pathogen and host, respectively (74% and 45% of predicted B. cinerea gene models, respectively) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 3 and 4).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of transcripts influenced by pathogen genetic variation.

claim: 5244 B. cinerea transcripts were significantly influenced by genetic variation in the host.
source: Of the 9284 detectable B. cinerea transcripts, 8603 and 5244 transcripts were significantly influenced by genetic variation in pathogen and host, respectively (74% and 45% of predicted B. cinerea gene models, respectively) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 3 and 4).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of transcripts influenced by host genetic variation.

claim: The variation in host defense responses (average H2Host = 0.010) has far less influence on B. cinerea gene expression than the pathogen's own natural genetic variation (average H2Isolate = 0.152).
source: While this result shows that the plant phytohormone pathways influence B. cinerea gene expression, the variation in host defense responses (average H2Host = 0.010) has far less influence on B. cinerea gene expression than that of the pathogens' own natural genetic variation (average H2Isolate = 0.152).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides heritability values comparing host and pathogen effects.

claim: 4541 B. cinerea genes showed genotype-by-genotype dependent expression (39% of B. cinerea predicted gene models, average H2Isolate x Host = 0.116).
source: The host defense hormones also affected B. cinerea gene expression in a genotype-by-genotype dependent manner on 4541 genes (39% of B. cinerea predicted gene models, average H2Isolate x Host = 0.116) (Figure 2B–2I).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of genes showing interaction effects with heritability values.

claim: Bcpg1 encodes an endopolygalacturonase gene.
source: The model-corrected means (log2) for the transcript of Bcpg1 (Bcin14g00850.1) encoding an endopolygalacturonase gene are utilized for plotting.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the function of Bcpg1.

claim: Bcoah encodes an oxaloacetate hydrolase gene.
source: The model-corrected means (log2) for the transcript of Bcoah (Bcin12g01020.1) encoding an oxaloacetate hydrolase gene are utilized for plotting.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the function of Bcoah.

claim: 2521 B. cinerea genes (22% of predicted gene models) showed significant positive correlations with lesion area across three Arabidopsis genotypes (p-value<0.01).
source: We identified 2521 genes (22% of B. cinerea predicted gene models) with significant positive correlations and 114 genes (1% of B. cinerea predicted gene models) with significant negative correlations to lesion area across three Arabidopsis genotypes, respectively (p-value<0.01, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of genes with positive correlations to lesion area.

claim: 114 B. cinerea genes (1% of predicted gene models) showed significant negative correlations with lesion area across three Arabidopsis genotypes (p-value<0.01).
source: We identified 2521 genes (22% of B. cinerea predicted gene models) with significant positive correlations and 114 genes (1% of B. cinerea predicted gene models) with significant negative correlations to lesion area across three Arabidopsis genotypes, respectively (p-value<0.01, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of genes with negative correlations to lesion area.

claim: The top 20 positively correlated B. cinerea genes contained all seven genes involved in BOT biosynthesis.
source: The top 20 positively correlated B. cinerea genes contained all seven genes involved in BOT biosynthesis (Deighton et al., 2001; Colmenares et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2009; Rossi et al., 2011; Ascari et al., 2013; Porquier et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding with supporting citations.

claim: More than 30 genes of the top 100 lesion-correlated genes encode plant cell wall degrading enzymes.
source: In addition to phytotoxins, more than 30 genes of the top 100 lesion-correlated genes encode plant cell wall degrading enzymes, that is glucosyl hydrolases, carbohydrate esterases, cellobiose dehydrogenases and Bcpg1 (Figure 3 and Figure 3—source data 1) (Gerbi et al., 1996; Zamocky et al., 2006; Cantarel et al., 2009; Van Vu et al., 2012; Igarashi et al., 2014; Morgenstern et al., 2014; Blanco-Ulate et al., 2014; Tan et al., 2015; Courtade et al., 2016; Nelson et al., 2017; Pérez‐Izquierdo et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding with supporting citations.

claim: 10 of the top 100 lesion-correlated genes were annotated as putative peptidase activities.
source: Additionally, 10 of the top 100 lesion-correlated genes were annotated as putative peptidase activities, which are critical for fungal virulence (Movahedi et al., 1991; Poussereau et al., 2001a; Poussereau et al., 2001b; ten Have et al., 2004; ten Have et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding with supporting citations.

claim: 37 of the top 100 lesion-correlated genes have no gene ontology (GO) terms.
source: In addition, this method identified 37 of the top 100 lesion-correlated genes with no gene ontology (GO) terms, which likely represent unknown virulence mechanisms (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding.

claim: Ten distinct B. cinerea GCNs containing more than five genes were identified.
source: We identified ten distinct GCNs containing more than five B. cinerea genes (Figure 5, Supplementary file 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the identification of ten GCNs.

claim: The largest B. cinerea GCN contains 242 genes associated with phospholipid synthesis, eiosome function, and membrane-associated stress signaling pathways.
source: The largest GCN with 242 genes contains members responsible for phospholipid synthesis, eiosome function, and membrane-associated stress signaling pathways (Figure 5-Vesicle/virulence).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the largest GCN and its functional associations.

claim: The second largest B. cinerea network contains 128 genes entirely associated with translation and protein synthesis.
source: The second largest network contains 128 genes that were entirely associated with translation and protein synthesis (Figure 5-TSL/growth and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the second largest GCN.

claim: Five B. cinerea GCNs were identified with genes distributed across B. cinerea 16 chromosomes, suggesting trans-regulation.
source: Of the smaller GCNs identified (5–20 genes), five networks were identified with genes distributed across B. cinerea 16 chromosomes, suggesting that these GCNs arise from coordinated trans-regulation (Figure 5-Trans-networks and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, F and H–J).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and provides an inference about trans-regulation.

claim: Three B. cinerea GCNs were predominantly comprised of genes tandemly clustered within a single chromosome.
source: In contrast to the whole-genome distributed GCNs, three of the smaller GCNs were predominantly comprised of genes tandemly clustered within a single chromosome with no or a few genes on other chromosomes (Figure 5-BOA, -Cyclic Peptide, -BOT, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, E and G).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes these clustered GCNs.

claim: Seven genes responsible for BOT biosynthesis cluster on chromosome 12 and form a small GCN with a Zn(II)2Cys6 transcription factor.
source: For example, seven genes responsible for BOT biosynthesis cluster on chromosome 12 and form a small GCN with a Zn(II)2Cys6 transcription factor that is specific to the pathway (Figure 6A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G and Figure 5—source data 1) (Siewers et al., 2005; Pinedo et al., 2008; Urlacher and Girhard, 2012; Moraga et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the BOT biosynthesis gene cluster with supporting citations.

claim: All 13 genes involved in BOA biosynthesis cluster in Chromosome one and form a highly connected GCN.
source: Similarly, all 13 genes involved in BOA biosynthesis cluster in Chromosome one and form a highly connected GCN (Figure 5-BOA, Figure 6E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and Figure 5—source data 1) (Dalmais et al., 2011; Porquier et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the BOA biosynthesis gene cluster with supporting citations.

claim: An uncharacterized set of ten genes cluster on Chromosome 1 and share homology with enzymes related to cyclic peptide biosynthesis.
source: In addition to previously characterized secondary metabolic pathways, we identified an uncharacterized set of ten genes that cluster on Chromosome 1 (Figure 5-Cyclic Peptide, Figure 6F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and Figure 5—source data 1). These genes share considerable homology with enzymes related to cyclic peptide biosynthesis and may represent a novel secondary metabolic pathway in B. cinerea (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this novel gene cluster and speculates about its function.

claim: Isolate 94.4 was the sole genotype lacking the entire BOT pathway.
source: Isolate 94.4 was the sole genotype lacking the entire BOT pathway, while 19 isolates and 24 isolates did not transcribe respectively the BOA and the putative cyclic peptide pathways (Figure 6E–6G and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding.

claim: 19 isolates did not transcribe the BOA pathway.
source: Isolate 94.4 was the sole genotype lacking the entire BOT pathway, while 19 isolates and 24 isolates did not transcribe respectively the BOA and the putative cyclic peptide pathways (Figure 6E–6G and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding.

claim: 24 isolates did not transcribe the putative cyclic peptide pathway.
source: Isolate 94.4 was the sole genotype lacking the entire BOT pathway, while 19 isolates and 24 isolates did not transcribe respectively the BOA and the putative cyclic peptide pathways (Figure 6E–6G and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding.

claim: There is a significant relationship between the expression of BOT and BOA pathways and lesion area measured at 72HPI.
source: This showed a significant relationship between the expression of BOT and BOA pathways and lesion area measured at 72HPI (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this statistical finding.

claim: The putative cyclic peptide pathway was only associated with lesion development in a BOT-dependent manner.
source: In contrast, the putative cyclic peptide pathway was only associated with lesion development in a BOT-dependent manner, suggesting that it may have a synergism to BOT (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and provides an inference about synergism.

source: Comparing the B. cinerea GCN membership and structure across the three Arabidopsis genotypes (WT, coi1-1, and npr1-1) showed that the core membership within networks was largely maintained but the specific linkages within and between GCNs were often variable (Figure 7, Supplementary file 1, Figure 7—figure supplements 1, 2 and 3, and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the comparison of GCN structure across genotypes.

claim: The two largest B. cinerea GCNs in WT developed multiple co-expression connections during infection in the JA-compromised coi1-1 host.
source: For example, the two largest B. cinerea GCNs in WT developed multiple co-expression connections during infection in the JA-compromised coi1-1 host (Figure 7 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this change in GCN structure.

source: This approach identified three cross-kingdom GCNs (CKGCNs) under Arabidopsis WT and JA- or SA-compromised two mutants (Figure 8, Supplementary file 5, and Figure 8—source data 1).

claim: Under Arabidopsis WT, a total of 54 hub genes were identified in CKGCNs, half from B. cinerea and half from Arabidopsis.
source: Under Arabidopsis WT, a total of 54 hub genes were identified, half from B. cinerea and half from Arabidopsis.

source: For plants, CKGCNs contain a majority of genes from Arabidopsis Defense/camalexin GCN (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding.

source: Of the host-derived GCNs, the Arabidopsis Defense/camalexin and Photosystem I (PSI) GCNs have a higher degree of centrality than do the Cell Division or Plastid GCNs across all three host genotypes, suggesting that they have the most interactions with B. cinerea GCNs.

source: However, the host genotype can change these GCN relationships. In the npr1-1 host, the host Defense/camalexin and PSI GCNs shift to a positive correlation.

source: This may reflect a shift in how the B. cinerea BOT GCN has a positive correlation with the Defense/camalexin GCN in the Col-0 host but a negative correlation in the npr1-1 host genotype.

source: Four independent biological replicates across two separate experiments per isolate/genotype pair were harvested at 16HPI for transcriptome analysis.

source: Plants have evolved a sophisticated set of constitutive and inducible immune responses to cope with constant selective pressures from antagonistic microbes (Jones and Dangl, 2006).

source: Reciprocally, plant pathogens have also evolved a variety of different invasion and virulence strategies to disarm or circumvent plant defense strategies (Glazebrook, 2005; Toruño et al., 2016).

source: For instance, Arabidopsis utilizes a complex signaling network to regulate the production of indole-derived secondary metabolites, such as camalexin and indole glucosinolates, that contribute to resistance against pathogens (Kliebenstein et al., 2005; Clay et al., 2009; Bednarek et al., 2009; Frerigmann et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2016; Mine et al., 2018).

source: For example, the biotrophic bacterial pathogen Pseudomonas syringae can utilize the jasmonic acid (JA) signaling pathway through the production of a JA-mimic, coronatine, to enhance its fitness (Mittal and Davis, 1995; Brooks et al., 2005; Cui et al., 2018).

source: In addition, pathogens can directly resist downstream defenses as is done by B. cinerea, where it has an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter BcatrB that provides resistance by exporting camalexin from the pathogen cell (Stefanato et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript states this with a supporting citation.

claim: B. cinerea secretes phytotoxic secondary metabolites, including the sesquiterpene botrydial (BOT) and the polyketide botcinic acid (BOA) that trigger plant chlorosis and host cell collapse.
source: For example, a key virulence mechanism is the secretion of phytotoxic secondary metabolites, including the sesquiterpene botrydial (BOT) and the polyketide botcinic acid (BOA) that trigger plant chlorosis and host cell collapse (Deighton et al., 2001; Colmenares et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2009; Rossi et al., 2011; Ascari et al., 2013; Porquier et al., 2016).

evidence: The manuscript states this with supporting citations.

claim: The B. cinerea collection includes the well-studied B05.10 isolate.

evidence: The manuscript explicitly mentions the B05.10 isolate.

source: The three Arabidopsis genotypes used in this study included the WT and two well-characterized immunodeficient mutants, coi1-1 and npr1-1, that abolish the major JA- or SA-defense perception pathways, respectively (Cao et al., 1997; Xie et al., 1998; Xu, 2002; Pieterse and Van Loon, 2004).
